items.sentence_raw: Over the past century, a powerful idea has taken root in the educational landscape.

The concept of intelligence as something innate has been supplanted by the idea that intelligence is not fixed, and that, with the right training, we can be the authors of our own cognitive capabilities.
Psychologist Alfred Binet, the developer of the first intelligence tests, was one of many 19th-century scientists who held that earlier view and sought to quantify cognitive ability.
items.explain: Q19: Alfred Binet was a scientist who *'held that earlier view'* — the view that intelligence is **innate** and fixed. **'Innate'** means an **unchangeable feature** you are born with. So the statement matches **A**.

items.sentence_raw: Then, in the early 20th century, progressive thinkers revolted against the notion that inherent ability is destiny.
items.explain: Q14: The first paragraph says *'in the early 20th century, progressive thinkers revolted against the notion that inherent ability is destiny'* — this shows a **shift** in ideas. **'Revolted against'** means they started to change their thinking. So the paragraph tells us **when** ideas about intelligence began to shift. The answer is **B**.

items.sentence_raw: Instead, educators such as John Dewey argued that every child's intelligence could be developed, given the right environment.
'Growth mindset theory' is a relatively new - and extremely popular - version of this idea.
In many schools today you will see hallways covered in motivational posters and hear speeches on the mindset of great sporting heroes who simply believed their way to the top.
A major focus of the growth mindset in schools is coaxing students away from seeing failure as an indication of their ability, and towards seeing it as a chance to improve that ability.
items.explain: Q15: The second paragraph says schools focus on *'coaxing students away from seeing failure as an indication of their ability, and towards seeing it as a chance to improve'*. This means schools want students to believe they can get better — to have **confidence in their potential to succeed**. So the answer is **C**.

items.sentence_raw: As educationalist Jeff Howard noted several decades ago: "Smart is not something that you just are, smart is something that you can get."
The idea of the growth mindset is based on the work of psychologist Carol Dweck in California in the 1990s.
In one key experiment, Dweck divided a group of 10- to 12-year-olds into two groups.
All were told that they had achieved a high score on a test but the first group were praised for their intelligence in achieving this, while the others were praised for their effort.
The second group - those who had been instilled with a 'growth mindset' - were subsequently far more likely to put effort into future tasks.
Meanwhile, the former took on only those tasks that would not risk their sense of worth.
This group had inferred that success or failure is due to innate ability, and this 'fixed mindset' had led them to fear of failure and lack of effort.
items.explain: Q16: The third paragraph says students with a fixed mindset *'had led them to fear of failure and lack of effort'*. This means they are **afraid to push themselves** because they might fail. ***Option C is a trap*** — it talks about needing encouragement, but the passage says they avoid hard tasks due to fear. So the answer is **D**.

items.sentence_raw: Praising ability actually made the students perform worse, while praising effort emphasised that change was possible.

One of the greatest impediments to successfully implementing a growth mindset, however, is the education system itself: in many parts of the world, the school climate is obsessed with performance in the form of constant testing, analysing and ranking of students - a key characteristic of the fixed mindset.
Nor is it unusual for schools to create a certain cognitive dissonance, when they applaud the benefits of a growth mindset but then hand out fixed target grades in lessons based on performance.
Aside from the implementation problem, the original growth mindset research has also received harsh criticism.
The statistician Andrew Gelman claims that "their research designs have enough degrees of freedom that they could take their data to support just about any theory at all".
items.explain: Q17: Andrew Gelman says the research *'designs have enough degrees of freedom that they could take their data to support just about any theory at all'*. This means the **methodology** was not strict or controlled enough. So the statement matches **C**.

items.sentence_raw: Professor of Psychology Timothy Bates, who has been trying to replicate Dweck's work, is finding that the results are repeatedly null.
He notes that: "People with a growth mindset don't cope any better with failure...
Kids with the growth mindset aren't getting better grades, either before or after our intervention study."
items.explain: Q22: Timothy Bates notes that *'Kids with the growth mindset aren't getting better grades'*. **'Aren't getting better grades'** means there is **no effect on academic achievement**. So the statement matches **D**.

items.sentence_raw: Much of this criticism is not lost on Dweck, and she deserves great credit for responding to it and adapting her work accordingly.
items.explain: Q23: The passage says Dweck *'deserves great credit for responding to it and adapting her work accordingly'*. **'Deserves great credit'** means she handled it in an **admirable way**. So the answer is **YES**.

items.sentence_raw: In fact, she argues that her work has been misunderstood and misapplied in a range of ways.
items.explain: Q18: Carol Dweck argues that her work *'has been misunderstood and misapplied in a range of ways'*. **'Misunderstood'** means **'incorrectly interpreted'**. So the statement matches **B**.

items.sentence_raw: She has also expressed concerns that her theories are being misappropriated in schools by being conflated with the self-esteem movement: "For me the growth mindset is a tool for learning and improvement.
items.explain: Q21: Carol Dweck says the growth mindset is *'not just a vehicle for making children feel good'*. This means it is **not simply about boosting students' morale** — it has a deeper purpose for learning. So the statement matches **B**.

items.sentence_raw: It's not just a vehicle for making children feel good."
items.explain: Q21: Carol Dweck says the growth mindset is *'not just a vehicle for making children feel good'*. This means it is **not simply about boosting students' morale** — it has a deeper purpose for learning. So the statement matches **B**.

items.sentence_raw: But there is another factor at work here.
The failure to translate the growth mindset into the classroom might reflect a misunderstanding of the nature of teaching and learning itself.
Growth mindset supporters David Yeager and Gregory Walton claim that interventions should be delivered in a subtle way to maximise their effectiveness.
items.explain: Q20: David Yeager and Gregory Walton claim interventions *'should be delivered in a subtle way to maximise their effectiveness'*. **'Subtle way'** means doing it without students really noticing — promoting it **without students being aware of it**. So the statement matches **E**.

items.sentence_raw: They say that if adolescents perceive a teacher's intervention as conveying that they are in need of help, this could undo its intended effects.
A lot of what drives students is their innate beliefs and how they perceive themselves.
There is a strong correlation between self-perception and achievement, but there is evidence to suggest that the actual effect of achievement on self-perception is stronger than the other way round.
items.explain: Q24: The passage says *'the actual effect of achievement on self-perception is stronger than the other way round'*. This means actual achievement is a **more effective driver** than self-perception — the question says the opposite. So the answer is **NO**.

items.sentence_raw: To stand up in a classroom and successfully deliver a good speech is a genuine achievement, and that is likely to be more powerfully motivating than vague notions of 'motivation' itself.
Recent evidence would suggest that growth mindset interventions are not the elixir of student learning that its proponents claim it to be.
The growth mindset appears to be a viable construct in the lab, which, when administered in the classroom via targeted interventions, doesn't seem to work.
It is hard to dispute that having faith in the capacity to change is a good attribute for students.
Paradoxically, however, that aspiration is not well served by direct interventions that try to instil it.
Motivational posters and talks are often a waste of time, and might well give students a deluded notion of what success actually means.
items.explain: Q26: The passage says *'Motivational posters and talks are often a waste of time, and might well give students a deluded notion of what success actually means'*. **'Deluded notion'** means a wrong idea, which is a **negative effect** of these deliberate attempts to encourage students. So the answer is **YES**.

items.sentence_raw: Teaching concrete skills such as how to write an effective introduction to an essay then praising students' effort in getting there is probably a far better way of improving confidence than telling them how unique they are, or indeed how capable they are of changing their own brains.
Perhaps growth mindset works best as a philosophy and not an intervention.

orphan_explain_map.25: Q25: The passage discusses recent evidence and criticism of growth mindset interventions. But it never mentions anything about **media coverage** — whether it was fair or unfair. ***NOT GIVEN is not the same as FALSE*** — the information is simply missing. So the answer is **NOT GIVEN**.
